From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer-Side Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## Preliminary points

**1. The "FINAL / not to be re-opened" label.** The Seller's preamble says these positions "were settled at principal level by both deal teams" and are not to be re-opened. Nothing else in front of me supports that. Please confirm with your principals before treating any point as conceded. Several positions also contradict the Seller's own Disclosure Letter, so they cannot be settled terms. The "market standard" ranges are advocacy, not a reason to accept any term. Even where a headline number is in a normal range, its effect depends on how it combines with disclosure, knowledge and scope, and here those combine badly.

**2. The Seller Update and the Disclosure Letter contradict each other.** This is useful leverage.

| Topic | Seller Update says | Disclosure Letter says |
|---|---|---|
| Bluefen | Consent is "addressed" | No final written consent; conditions not shown as satisfied |
| Riverlark | Release to follow Completion | Not repaid; no discharge of security |
| Ironquay | Indemnity "adequate" | No payment receipt, no confirmatory assignment, AUD 180k open |
| DD-006 | "Not expected to be material" | Access, scope and notification obligation all unknown |
| Sandbar | Ordinary course | Silent on ordinary course, terminability and accrual |

**3. The disclosure is stale.** It speaks as at 22 September 2026. Today is 5 November 2026. Six weeks of developments (Bluefen, DD-006, Riverlark) are not reflected.

**Caveat:** I have only the Seller's summary positions, not the full SPA text. My recommendations should be checked against the actual clause drafting and the full DD record.

---

## Material issues

### A. Price mechanics (debt-free / cash-free): highest priority, money out of our pocket

**A1. Riverlark facility (about AUD 3.2m), Clause 2/7**
- The deal is debt-free/cash-free. A release "following Completion" means we would pay a full AUD 24m price for a company still carrying AUD 3.2m of secured debt.
- The change of control under facility cl 8.1 is likely to trigger a default or prepayment event at Completion. Discharge mechanics sit in cl 9.2.
- **Push back:**
  - The facility must be repaid at Completion out of the price, under a payout letter agreed before Completion.
  - Executed deeds of release and discharge of all security, plus PPSR release undertakings, must be a Completion deliverable.
  - Riverlark debt should be expressly defined as Indebtedness deducted from the price.
  - Check whether the Seller or any group entity has given share security or guarantees that also need release.

**A2. DD-005 closing bonuses (AUD 420,000)**
- The Seller calls these "a matter for the Seller" but leaves them out of the funds flow. The obligations sit with the Company as employer, so we would bear them after Completion.
- Payroll tax, superannuation guarantee and on-costs (and PAYG withholding mechanics) are unaddressed. The true cost exceeds AUD 420k.
- **Push back:**
  - Treat the bonuses plus all on-costs as Transaction Expenses or Indebtedness, deducted from the price.
  - Pay them through payroll at or immediately after Completion, funded by the Seller.
  - Add a specific indemnity, outside cap and basket, for any shortfall or related tax and super liability.

**A3. Sandbar renewals (3 × AUD 110,000 = AUD 330,000)**
- Three "related" renewals of identical value, which the Seller itself says should be "read together for timing/scope", look like one commitment split into three. That pattern could keep each contract under an interim-period consent threshold or approval limit. Each is below the AUD 250k basket, but the total is not.
- The disclosure is silent on whether they are ordinary course, terminable, prepaid or accrued, and on whether Sandbar is a related party of the Seller.
- **Push back:**
  - Require full contracts, timing and approval records.
  - Require confirmation of whether Sandbar is related to Harbourglass.
  - If the renewals were not ordinary course, or were entered after signing or near the deal, either:
    - have them terminated at Seller cost before Completion,
    - treat any unpaid committed amounts as debt-like, or
    - obtain a specific indemnity.
  - Tighten the conduct-of-business covenant to aggregate related contracts.

### B. Conditions precedent

**B1. Bluefen consent, Clause 3/6.3 (about AUD 3.6m, about 30% of FY26 revenue)**
- This is the most commercially significant customer issue. Losing Bluefen goes to the core of the valuation.
- The Seller's mechanism has three problems:
  - "Reasonable endeavours" is too weak.
  - The condition is satisfied on mere "delivery of the counterparty's written consent", even if that consent is conditional.
  - The cl 11.3 conditions are not addressed at all.
- **Push back:**
  - Make it a hard Condition Precedent for the Buyer's benefit, waivable only by the Buyer.
  - Raise the standard to all reasonable endeavours, with Buyer involvement in communications.
  - The consent must be unconditional, or its cl 11.3 conditions satisfied, in a form reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer, with no adverse amendment to the contract.
  - Include a long-stop date with a Buyer termination right.
  - Consider a price adjustment or earn-out holdback if Bluefen gives notice within a set period after Completion.

**B2. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)**
- These are lower risk, but the Seller's own characterisation is unverified. Confirm whether either document defines a change of control as a deemed assignment.
- Require the lease notification to be given, with evidence, before Completion. Add a warranty that no consent is triggered by the transaction.

### C. Specific indemnities

**C1. Ironquay IP, Clause 11.1**
- Under DD-004 cl 7.3, title to the SOW3 Project Materials passes only on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. AUD 180k is shown open (DD-010), there is no payment evidence and no assignment.
- The real risk is that the Company does not own IP in its product, with consequent infringement or licensing exposure. The risk is not the AUD 180k payment itself. An indemnity capped at the SOW3 payment misses the exposure.
- **Push back:**
  - Make it a Completion deliverable that the SOW3 fees are paid (with bank evidence) and that Ironquay executes a confirmatory IP assignment and moral rights consent.
  - Failing that, require a broad indemnity for all loss arising from any defect in the Company's title to or right to use the SOW3 materials, outside cap, basket and general time limits.
  - Consider a retention or escrow.

**C2. DD-006 export/privacy incident, Clause 4.6/Schedule 6**
- About 1,240 personal records were sent to an unintended external address. Access, scope and notification obligations were still unknown as at 22 September.
- Under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity must carry out a reasonable assessment of a suspected eligible data breach, generally within 30 days. By now that window has very likely passed. Either an assessment exists and should be disclosed, or the Company may be out of compliance. "Not expected to be material" is an assertion with no basis in the record.
- **Push back:**
  - Require the current investigation file, the assessment outcome, and any OAIC or individual notification decisions and correspondence.
  - Require a specific indemnity for all costs, claims, remediation, regulatory response and third-party loss arising from the incident, outside cap and basket, with a longer survival period.
  - Note that recovery of regulatory penalties under an indemnity may be limited on public-policy grounds. Confirm the drafting approach with litigation and privacy counsel.
  - Add warranties that there have been no other incidents and that the Company complies with the APPs.

### D. Limitation regime: the combined effect guts protection

**D1. Fundamental warranties (title and capacity) treated as general warranties**
- This is unacceptable. Title is the asset we are buying. A 20% cap and 18 months means we could pay AUD 24m and recover only AUD 4.8m if the shares are not owned.
- **Push back:** cap at 100% of the price, a survival period of at least 6–7 years, and no basket or de minimis.

**D2. Title evidence (DD-012)**
- The share register alone is insufficient. The Seller's own letter notes the Buyer has not verified title.
- **Push back:** require:
  - an ASIC company extract consistent with the register,
  - original share certificates or a lost-certificate indemnity,
  - PPSR searches against the Company and Seller,
  - confirmation that there are no options, convertible notes, ESOP rights or other securities,
  - evidence of all historical share issues and transfers.

**D3. Tax**
- "Settled under the general regime" means tax exposures would sit under a 20% cap and 18 months. That is far shorter than ATO amendment periods, which are generally 4 years for companies and unlimited for fraud or evasion.
- **Push back:** require a separate tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax, including payroll tax and super on the bonuses. The cap should be at least 100% of the price, with survival matching amendment periods plus a buffer (for example 6–7 years).

**D4. IP warranties.** Given C1, the core IP ownership warranties should be fundamental, or at least carry a higher cap and longer survival.

**D5. Clause 9.3/12.8/20.5: "all Claims of any nature" and Clause 13 "unless expressly stated"**
- As drafted, the caps, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance provisions would capture:
  - specific indemnities,
  - the tax indemnity,
  - fundamental warranties,
  - covenants and Completion obligations,
  - price adjustment and leakage,
  - fraud.
- **Push back:**
  - Limitations apply to general Warranty Claims only. Indemnities, tax, fundamental warranties, covenants and price mechanics are carved out unless expressly stated.
  - Include an express carve-out for fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller, its officers and its advisers.
  - Ensure non-reliance does not purport to exclude claims for misleading or deceptive conduct under the Australian Consumer Law (s 18) in a way that is either unenforceable or overreaching. At minimum, preserve reliance on the Warranties and the Disclosure Letter itself.

**D6. Headline cap, basket and de minimis (Clause 12.1/12.2)**
- A 20% cap (AUD 4.8m) is arguable if everything else is fixed. Consider W&I insurance as a route to a higher effective cap.
- The basket is drafted as a deductible ("only the excess"). Push for a tipping basket, meaning recovery from the first dollar once the threshold is met. Also push for a lower threshold (for example 0.5%, or AUD 120k).
- Push the de minimis down (for example AUD 10k), with related claims aggregated so that a series of linked small claims counts as one.
- On survival, push general warranties to 24 months, so that at least one full audit cycle after Completion falls inside the period.

### E. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge: the most dangerous structural combination

**E1. General disclosure of the entire data room and public registers (DL [1.1]–[1.2])**
- This lets the Seller argue that anything buried anywhere in DD-002 to DD-012, or in any public record, qualifies every warranty.
- **Push back:**
  - Reject general disclosure.
  - Only specific disclosures, made fairly and with sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter, should qualify the warranties.
  - Each disclosure should be cross-referenced to the warranties it qualifies.
  - Disclosures should not qualify the fundamental warranties, tax warranties or any indemnity.

**E2. Buyer knowledge, Clause 8.3**
- The clause covers the Buyer *or its advisers* and anything *discoverable*. It is constructive-knowledge anti-sandbagging, and combined with E1 it renders the warranties close to worthless.
- **Push back:**
  - Preferred position: the Buyer's rights are not affected by any knowledge, actual, constructive or imputed, other than matters fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter.
  - Fallback: limit to the actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals, as at signing, of the specific breach. Exclude advisers and constructive knowledge.
  - In all cases, knowledge never qualifies indemnities, tax or fundamental warranties.

**E3. Staleness and bring-down**
- **Push back:**
  - The warranties are repeated at Completion.
  - Any supplemental disclosure before Completion does not cure a breach for damages purposes, but gives the Buyer a termination right if the matter is material.
  - The Seller must deliver an updated Disclosure Letter now, covering developments since 22 September.

---

## Summary of recommendations

**Must-haves (deal-critical):**
1. **Riverlark:** repay at Completion from the price under a payout letter, with security releases delivered at Completion. Reject a post-Completion release.
2. **Bonuses:** deduct the AUD 420k plus all payroll tax, super and on-costs from the price, and back this with an indemnity.
3. **Bluefen:** make it a hard, Buyer-only waivable CP, requiring unconditional consent (or satisfied cl 11.3 conditions), all reasonable endeavours, and a long-stop termination right.
4. **Fundamental warranties (title and capacity):** 100% cap, 6–7 years survival, no thresholds, no disclosure or knowledge qualification. Verify title with ASIC, PPSR, certificates and a cap-table check.
5. **Limitation scope:** limitations apply to general Warranty Claims only. Carve out fraud, indemnities, tax, fundamental warranties, covenants and price mechanics.
6. **Disclosure and knowledge:** reject general data room and public register disclosure. Specific, fair disclosure only. Strike or narrow constructive-knowledge anti-sandbagging.

**Strongly required:**
7. **Ironquay:** require a paid-fee evidence and confirmatory IP assignment as a CP or deliverable. Otherwise a full IP-title indemnity outside caps, plus a retention.
8. **DD-006:** obtain current NDB assessment status and records, plus a specific uncapped (or separately capped) privacy indemnity with longer survival.
9. **Tax:** a stand-alone tax indemnity with survival aligned to ATO amendment periods.
10. **Sandbar:** require full documents and related-party confirmation. Terminate, treat as debt-like, or indemnify if not ordinary course. Aggregate related contracts in the interim covenants.

**Negotiable / tactical:**
11. Push for a tipping basket at a lower threshold, de minimis around AUD 10k with aggregation, and 24-month survival for general warranties.
12. Accept a 20% general cap only as a trade for the points above, or explore W&I insurance.
13. Require an updated Disclosure Letter now, a Completion bring-down, and a rule that supplemental disclosure does not cure breaches.
14. Confirm the lease notification is given, and confirm no change-of-control trigger in the lease or under Mossvale.

**Process:** Do not treat any position as agreed until your principals confirm it. Use the inconsistencies between the Seller Update and its own Disclosure Letter as the opening point in the mark-up response.

I can turn this into a clause-by-clause mark-up or an issues list for the Seller once we have the full SPA text.

  - Include an express carve-out for fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller, its officers and its advisers.
  - Ensure non-reliance does not purport to exclude claims for misleading or deceptive conduct under the Australian Consumer Law (s 18) in a way that is either unenforceable or overreaching. At minimum, preserve reliance on the Warranties and the Disclosure Letter itself.

**D6. Headline cap, basket and de minimis (Clause 12.1/12.2)**
- A 20% cap (AUD 4.8m) is arguable if everything else is fixed. Consider W&I insurance as a route to a higher effective cap.
- The basket is drafted as a deductible ("only the excess"). Push for a tipping basket, meaning recovery from the first dollar once the threshold is met. Also push for a lower threshold (for example 0.5%, or AUD 120k).
- Push the de minimis down (for example AUD 10k), with related claims aggregated so that a series of linked small claims counts as one.
- On survival, push general warranties to 24 months, so that at least one full audit cycle after Completion falls inside the period.

### E. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge: the most dangerous structural combination

**E1. General disclosure of the entire data room and public registers (DL [1.1]–[1.2])**
- This lets the Seller argue that anything buried anywhere in DD-002 to DD-012, or in any public record, qualifies every warranty.
- **Push back:**
  - Reject general disclosure.
  - Only specific disclosures, made fairly and with sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter, should qualify the warranties.
  - Each disclosure should be cross-referenced to the warranties it qualifies.
  - Disclosures should not qualify the fundamental warranties, tax warranties or any indemnity.

**E2. Buyer knowledge, Clause 8.3**
- The clause covers the Buyer *or its advisers* and anything *discoverable*. It is constructive-knowledge anti-sandbagging, and combined with E1 it renders the warranties close to worthless.
- **Push back:**
  - Preferred position: the Buyer's rights are not affected by any knowledge, actual, constructive or imputed, other than matters fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter.
  - Fallback: limit to the actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals, as at signing, of the specific breach. Exclude advisers and constructive knowledge.
  - In all cases, knowledge never qualifies indemnities, tax or fundamental warranties.

**E3. Staleness and bring-down**
- **Push back:**
  - The warranties are repeated at Completion.
  - Any supplemental disclosure before Completion does not cure a breach for damages purposes, but gives the Buyer a termination right if the matter is material.
  - The Seller must deliver an updated Disclosure Letter now, covering developments since 22 September.
